question: Why is studying medical parasitology important for midwives practicing in Nigeria?

options.A: Viruses and fungi are classified as parasites in local curricula
options.B: Developed nations have completely eradicated all forms of human worms
options.C: Parasitic infections heavily contribute to maternal health issues and childhood malnutrition locally
options.D: Laboratory machines require daily manual calibration by midwives

explanation: High burdens of conditions like malaria and intestinal worms directly impact vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and children in our environment. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which type of relationship describes one organism benefiting while the other is completely unaffected?

options.A: Predation
options.B: Mutualism
options.C: Commensalism
options.D: Parasitism

explanation: In commensalism, one party gains an advantage while the host experiences neither positive nor negative effects. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h2)

question: How does parasitism fundamentally differ from mutualism?

options.A: Parasitism causes harm to the host, whereas mutualism provides benefits to both organisms
options.B: Mutualistic relationships are temporary, while parasitic ones last a lifetime
options.C: Hosts always die in a parasitic relationship but survive in mutualism
options.D: Parasites are always microscopic, while mutualistic partners are large

explanation: The key difference is the outcome for the host: damage and exploitation versus shared advantages. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which of the following organisms is classified as a protozoan?

options.A: Taenia solium
options.B: Ascaris lumbricoides
options.C: Sarcoptes scabiei
options.D: Plasmodium species

explanation: Plasmodium, the parasite that causes malaria, is a single-celled microscopic protozoan. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h3)

question: What main feature separates helminths from protozoa?

options.A: Helminths live on the skin, whereas protozoa live in the blood
options.B: Protozoa can be seen clearly with the naked eye
options.C: Protozoa have rigid cell walls made of chitin
options.D: Helminths are multicellular worms, whereas protozoa are single-celled

explanation: Helminths are complex, many-celled worms, while protozoa consist of only a single microscopic cell. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the main characteristic of a parasite with a direct life cycle?

options.A: It reproduces exclusively through soil contact
options.B: It requires only a single host species to complete its development
options.C: It cannot survive outside of human blood
options.D: It must pass through an insect before reaching a human

explanation: Direct transmission means the organism moves from one host to another without needing an intermediate animal or insect host. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h4)

question: A patient contracts malaria after being bitten by an infected female Anopheles mosquito. What role does the mosquito play?

options.A: Mechanical carrier without development
options.B: Definitive host only
options.C: Intermediate host and vector
options.D: Accidental dead-end host

explanation: The mosquito serves as the vector transmitting the parasite and hosts the sexual stages of the Plasmodium life cycle. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which parasitic infection is a leading cause of severe anaemia among pregnant women in Nigeria due to chronic blood loss?

options.A: Amoebiasis
options.B: Toxoplasmosis
options.C: Hookworm
options.D: Pinworm

explanation: Hookworms attach to the intestinal wall and feed on host blood, frequently causing significant iron-deficiency anaemia in endemic regions. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why does Plasmodium falciparum malaria pose such a high clinical risk in tropical healthcare settings?

options.A: It affects exclusively adult males
options.B: It rapidly causes severe systemic complications like profound anaemia and organ involvement
options.C: It is completely resistant to all rapid test kits
options.D: It spreads through airborne droplets in maternity wards

explanation: Plasmodium falciparum is the most virulent malaria species, capable of causing rapid and life-threatening complications if untreated. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h5)

question: Which diagnostic method is most commonly used for a quick check of malaria antigens in a busy antenatal clinic?

options.A: Rapid Diagnostic Test
options.B: Polymerase Chain Reaction
options.C: Liver biopsy and histology
options.D: Stool culture on agar plates

explanation: RDTs provide fast, reliable antigen detection at the point of care without needing a complex laboratory setup. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of examining a wet mount stool preparation under a microscope?

options.A: To measure the patient's hemoglobin level
options.B: To detect ova, cysts, or active protozoan trophozoites
options.C: To identify viral loads in the bloodstream
options.D: To culture bacteria causing bowel infections

explanation: Stool microscopy allows laboratory scientists to visualize intestinal parasite eggs, cysts, or moving trophozoites directly. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why does malaria infection during pregnancy pose a direct threat to fetal development?

options.A: Fetal red blood cells are the primary targets for rupture
options.B: Parasites collect in the placenta, impairing oxygen and nutrient transfer
options.C: The infection halts maternal production of amniotic fluid
options.D: Malaria parasites invade the fetal brain during the first trimester

explanation: Placental malaria restricts fetal growth by disrupting blood flow and nutrient exchange across the placental interface. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h7)

question: A pregnant woman attending antenatal clinic at 24 weeks gestation is prescribed sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. What is the primary clinical goal?

options.A: Prevention of congenital syphilis transmission
options.B: Routine eradication of intestinal hookworms
options.C: Emergency treatment for acute cerebral malaria
options.D: Intermittent Preventive Treatment for malaria

explanation: IPTp-SP is administered at routine intervals during pregnancy to reduce the burden of malaria and its adverse outcomes. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T3#BMP116_U3_T3_h7)

question: What is the main difference that separates protozoa from bacteria?

options.A: The total absence of any genetic material
options.B: A defined nucleus and organelles
options.C: A rigid outer peptidoglycan wall
options.D: A capsule made of thick polysaccharide

explanation: Protozoa are eukaryotic cells, meaning they have a true membrane-bound nucleus and internal parts, unlike bacteria which are prokaryotic. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why is learning about single-celled parasites so important for everyday midwifery practice in Nigeria?

options.A: They are the sole cause of all maternal infections
options.B: They can only be observed using electron microscopes
options.C: Protozoa respond instantly to standard antibacterial drugs
options.D: Vector-borne protozoan diseases are highly prevalent locally

explanation: Nigeria has a high number of parasitic infections like malaria, making clinical knowledge of protozoa something midwives use regularly. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which type of Plasmodium causes the most severe cases of malaria across Nigeria?

options.A: Plasmodium malariae
options.B: Plasmodium falciparum
options.C: Plasmodium knowlesi
options.D: Plasmodium vivax

explanation: Plasmodium falciparum is the most common type in sub-Saharan Africa and is known to cause severe clinical complications. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which malaria parasite species is known to stay dormant in the liver and cause relapses later?

options.A: Plasmodium vivax
options.B: Plasmodium knowlesi
options.C: Plasmodium falciparum
options.D: Plasmodium malariae

explanation: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale have liver stages that can remain inactive and trigger new episodes of illness weeks or months later. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h2)

question: What form of the malaria parasite does the female Anopheles mosquito pass into the human body?

options.A: Hypnozoite
options.B: Merozoite
options.C: Sporozoite
options.D: Gametocyte

explanation: Female mosquitoes carry sporozoites in their saliva and release them into the skin and blood when they bite a human. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h3)

question: What happens in the body right when infected red blood cells burst open?

options.A: The cessation of all parasite multiplication
options.B: Immediate development of long-lasting immunity
options.C: An acute paroxysm of chills and high fever
options.D: The permanent clearance of all liver parasites

explanation: When red blood cells burst together, they release waste and toxins that trigger sudden shaking chills and a high fever spike. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the main effect of cytoadherence in falciparum malaria?

options.A: Blocking of small blood vessels in vital organs
options.B: Enhancement of normal red blood cell production
options.C: Prevention of gametocyte formation in the liver
options.D: Rapid destruction of parasites within the human spleen

explanation: Cytoadherence makes infected red blood cells stick to blood vessel walls, keeping them away from the spleen but blocking normal blood flow. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h4)

question: How do infected red blood cells avoid being cleared out by the spleen?

options.A: Accelerated duplication of cellular DNA
options.B: Sequestration via surface knob adhesion
options.C: Rapid conversion into free-swimming sporozoites
options.D: Thickening of the outer leukocyte membrane

explanation: Surface changes help infected cells stick to blood vessel walls, keeping them away from the spleen where immune cells would normally destroy them. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why are pregnant women more likely to get severe malaria in areas where the disease is common?

options.A: Their bodies completely stop producing red blood cells
options.B: Mosquitoes are biologically attracted exclusively to pregnant skin
options.C: Gestation-related immunomodulation reduces their parasite defense
options.D: The parasite cannot survive outside the pregnant uterus

explanation: Normal immune system changes during pregnancy lower the body's defense against malaria, making it easier for the parasite to multiply. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h5)

question: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks feels fine, but routine screening shows heavy malaria infection. What explains this?

options.A: The parasite has transformed into a harmless commensal organism
options.B: Fetal hemoglobin actively neutralizes all circulating toxins
options.C: Laboratory reagents always produce false positives during pregnancy
options.D: Placental malaria can develop with minimal peripheral fever symptoms

explanation: Parasites can build up in the placenta while the mother shows very few signs of illness, which is why routine antenatal testing is so important. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h5)

question: Which stain is traditionally used to look for malaria parasites in blood smears under a microscope?

options.A: Acid-fast stain
options.B: Gram stain
options.C: Methylene blue stain
options.D: Giemsa stain

explanation: Giemsa stain is the standard laboratory stain used to highlight Plasmodium parasites inside red blood cells on blood slides. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why is it not recommended to rely only on a patient's symptoms to confirm malaria?

options.A: Symptoms of malaria closely resemble other common febrile illnesses
options.B: Parasites disappear completely before any clinical signs appear
options.C: Fever is never present in any stage of a protozoan infection
options.D: Laboratory tests are universally cheaper than physical exams

explanation: Signs like fever, headache, and chills look very similar to other illnesses like typhoid, so diagnostic tests are needed for confirmation. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h6)

question: Which medication is currently given to prevent malaria during pregnancy in Nigeria?

options.A: Artemether-Lumefantrine
options.B: Chloroquine phosphate
options.C: Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine
options.D: Intravenous Quinine

explanation: Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP) is the recommended medicine for Intermittent Preventive Treatment during pregnancy at scheduled antenatal visits. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h7)

question: When should a pregnant woman usually receive her first dose of preventive malaria treatment (IPTp-SP)?

options.A: Immediately upon confirming conception in the first week
options.B: Only during active labor in the delivery ward
options.C: Wait until the postpartum period after delivery
options.D: Early in the second trimester during routine antenatal care

explanation: IPTp-SP starts in the second trimester once the pregnancy is stable, and is continued at monthly intervals during clinic visits. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is a major problem for the baby that is directly linked to placental malaria?

options.A: Permanent neonatal blindness
options.B: Macrosomia and high birth weight
options.C: Low birth weight and fetal growth restriction
options.D: Congenital bone malformations

explanation: When malaria affects the placenta, it can reduce nutrient transfer to the baby, often resulting in babies born smaller than expected. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h8)

question: A pregnant first-time mother comes in with severe tiredness, paleness, and ongoing malaria. What condition is she most at risk of developing?

options.A: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.B: Severe maternal anemia
options.C: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Primary postpartum depression

explanation: The destruction of red blood cells by the parasite combined with reduced blood cell production puts pregnant women at high risk for severe anemia. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T4#BMP116_U3_T4_h8)

question: What type of living organisms are protozoa?

options.A: Single-celled microscopic parasites
options.B: Visible parasitic worms
options.C: Microscopic fungal spores
options.D: Multi-celled external insects

explanation: Protozoa are microscopic organisms made of only one cell that can survive as parasites inside human hosts. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why are pregnant women often more vulnerable to parasitic infections?

options.A: Their digestive tracts slow down to absorb more parasites
options.B: Their body temperature permanently rises to fight pathogens
options.C: Their immune systems undergo natural changes during pregnancy
options.D: They consume significantly more water than non-pregnant women

explanation: Normal physiological shifts in immunity during pregnancy lower the body's defense against certain infections. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which form of Entamoeba histolytica is responsible for surviving in the outside environment?

options.A: Cyst
options.B: Larva
options.C: Spore
options.D: Trophozoite

explanation: The cyst has a tough outer wall that allows it to survive outside the human body in soil or water for weeks. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h2)

question: How do humans primarily become infected with this parasite?

options.A: Direct skin contact with infected soil while farming
options.B: Ingesting food or water contaminated with cysts
options.C: Being bitten by infected mosquitoes during the rainy season
options.D: Inhaling airborne spores released from dry soil

explanation: Transmission happens via the fecal-oral route when a person swallows food or water polluted with microscopic cysts. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the classic shape of the tissue ulcers formed in the intestine by Entamoeba histolytica?

options.A: Flask-shaped
options.B: Long linear strips
options.C: Raised cauliflower bumps
options.D: Circular patches

explanation: The destructive enzymes of the trophozoites burrow deep into the mucosa, creating narrow necks that widen at the base, forming flask-shaped ulcers. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h3)

question: Where does the parasite usually travel first when it causes extra-intestinal disease?

options.A: Brain
options.B: Liver
options.C: Kidneys
options.D: Lungs

explanation: Parasites entering the portal circulation are filtered primarily by the liver, making it the most common site for extra-intestinal abscesses. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of amoebic dysentery?

options.A: Bright green vomiting after every meal
options.B: Stools containing blood and mucus
options.C: Complete inability to pass any stool
options.D: Profuse watery diarrhea without mucus

explanation: Tissue destruction in the colon causes bleeding and mucus production, resulting in bloody, mucous-laden stools. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why is severe gastroenteritis particularly dangerous for a pregnant patient?

options.A: It causes the amniotic fluid to completely dry up within hours
options.B: It stops the placenta from producing any progesterone instantly
options.C: Fluid loss and cramping can trigger uterine contractions and preterm labor
options.D: It automatically causes permanent blindness in the developing fetus

explanation: Severe dehydration, electrolyte shifts, and abdominal cramping put physical stress on the uterus, risking premature delivery. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h4)

question: Which diagnostic imaging method is safest for checking a pregnant woman for a liver abscess?

options.A: Standard X-ray of the abdomen
options.B: Abdominal ultrasound
options.C: Computed tomography (CT)
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

explanation: Ultrasound uses sound waves rather than ionizing radiation, making it safe and effective for evaluating hepatic lesions during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why are multiple stool samples sometimes requested when investigating intestinal parasites?

options.A: Laboratories require three samples to run blood sugar tests
options.B: The parasite is not always shed continuously in the feces
options.C: Pathogens multiply only during the night hours
options.D: Single samples are instantly destroyed by standard laboratory air

explanation: Because cyst and trophozoite output fluctuates, examining specimens over several days reduces the chance of a false-negative result. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of giving a luminal amoebicide after treating invasive disease?

options.A: To prevent the kidneys from retaining excess water and salt
options.B: To eliminate remaining cysts in the intestinal lumen and prevent relapse
options.C: To boost the red blood cell count lost during bloody diarrhea
options.D: To instantly dissolve deep abscesses located inside the liver tissue

explanation: Tissue amoebicides clear invasive forms, but luminal agents are needed to clear lingering cysts in the gut lumen to stop reinfection. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h6)

question: During which stage of pregnancy do clinicians exercise the highest caution when prescribing medications like metronidazole?

options.A: Third trimester
options.B: Second trimester
options.C: First trimester
options.D: Postpartum period

explanation: Organogenesis occurs in the first trimester, making the developing fetus most vulnerable to potential teratogenic drug effects. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is a major threat to fetal well-being during severe maternal dehydration?

options.A: Rapid increase in amniotic fluid volume
options.B: Premature closure of the fetal skull bones
options.C: Compromised placental blood flow
options.D: Instant calcification of the umbilical cord

explanation: Severe fluid loss reduces maternal blood volume, which lowers perfusion through the placenta and reduces oxygen delivery to the fetus. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct complication of severe, untreated invasive amoebiasis?

options.A: Intestinal perforation and peritonitis
options.B: Development of gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: Amoebic liver abscess formation
options.D: Preterm labor secondary to dehydration

explanation: Gestational diabetes is related to maternal insulin resistance and pancreatic function, not parasitic infection of the bowel or liver. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h7)

question: What is a key nursing action when managing a pregnant patient with severe diarrhea?

options.A: Monitoring fluid intake and output meticulously
options.B: Restricting all water intake to rest the bowel
options.C: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise
options.D: Stopping all handwashing to build natural immunity

explanation: Tracking fluid balance ensures that dehydration is detected early and corrected with oral or intravenous rehydration therapy. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h8)

question: Which health education message is most effective for preventing the spread of Entamoeba histolytica in a community?

options.A: Sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets every night without fail
options.B: Avoid eating all protein sources, including fish and lean meats
options.C: Take prophylactic metronidazole tablets every single week of the year
options.D: Wash hands thoroughly with soap after using the toilet and before eating

explanation: Interrupting the fecal-oral transmission cycle through hand hygiene and safe water practices is the most effective way to prevent infection. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T5#BMP116_U3_T5_h8)

question: How is Trichomonas vaginalis mainly spread from person to person?

options.A: Inhalation of airborne spores
options.B: Ingestion of contaminated food
options.C: Direct sexual contact
options.D: Contact with contaminated soil

explanation: The parasite is passed through direct contact during sexual intercourse because it cannot survive outside the human body for very long. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why can't Trichomonas vaginalis survive for a long time outside the human body?

options.A: It lacks a resistant cyst stage in its life cycle
options.B: It requires human body temperature to replicate its DNA
options.C: It depends entirely on dietary iron found only in blood
options.D: It is quickly destroyed by high levels of environmental oxygen

explanation: Without a tough outer shell or cyst stage to protect it, the parasite quickly dies when exposed to the outside environment. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h1)

question: What happens to the normal vaginal pH during a Trichomonas vaginalis infection?

options.A: It remains completely unchanged
options.B: It fluctuates strictly with the menstrual cycle
options.C: It drops to a highly acidic level
options.D: It increases above the normal acidic range

explanation: The activity of the parasite and a drop in protective bacteria cause the vagina to become less acidic than normal. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h2)

question: An active Trichomonas infection causes irritation in the vaginal tissues. What secondary health risk increases because of this?

options.A: Acquiring human immunodeficiency virus
options.B: Developing pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.C: Suffering from severe iron-deficiency anemia
options.D: Developing chronic gestational diabetes

explanation: Small sores and inflammation in the tissues provide an easier entry point for viruses like HIV, raising the risk of infection. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which physical sign on the cervix is commonly seen with a Trichomonas infection?

options.A: Extensive ulcerations resembling herpes lesions
options.B: A smooth, pale cervix with closed os
options.C: Strawberry cervix with punctate hemorrhages
options.D: A thick, white mucous plug blocking the os

explanation: Tiny red spots appear on the cervix due to irritated blood vessels, giving it a look that midwives often describe like a strawberry. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h3)

question: What type of vaginal discharge is most typical of trichomoniasis?

options.A: Clear, watery, and completely odorless
options.B: Dark brown, thick, and blood-tinged
options.C: Thick, white, and resembling cottage cheese
options.D: Frothy, yellow-green, and sometimes foul-smelling

explanation: A frothy, yellow-green discharge is a classic sign that helps distinguish trichomoniasis from other common vaginal infections. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which diagnostic test is currently the most accurate for detecting Trichomonas vaginalis?

options.A: Routine wet mount microscopy
options.B: Standard cervical cytology smear
options.C: Nucleic acid amplification tests
options.D: Potassium hydroxide whiff test

explanation: NAATs are the most sensitive tests because they detect the genetic material of the parasite even when only a small amount is present. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why is wet mount microscopy still widely used in busy primary health clinics in Nigeria despite lower accuracy?

options.A: It requires no specialized training or equipment whatsoever
options.B: It is completely foolproof with a hundred percent accuracy rate
options.C: It can definitively identify all co-existing viral infections
options.D: It provides immediate results during the clinical consultation

explanation: Wet mounts are affordable and give answers right away while the patient is still at the clinic, allowing treatment to start immediately. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which group of medications is mainly used to treat Trichomonas vaginalis infections?

options.A: Sulfa drugs
options.B: Aminoglycosides
options.C: Cephalosporins
options.D: Nitroimidazoles

explanation: Medications such as metronidazole belong to the nitroimidazole group and are the first-line treatment for this parasite. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why is it important to treat the sexual partner as well when managing trichomoniasis?

options.A: To restore normal estrogen levels in the female partner
options.B: To prevent rapid reinfection from untreated partners
options.C: To prevent the development of permanent pelvic scarring
options.D: To eradicate bacteria causing secondary yeast infections

explanation: Partners often carry the infection without showing symptoms, so treating them prevents the woman from catching it again right away. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h5)

question: How can an untreated Trichomonas infection increase the risk of preterm delivery in pregnant women?

options.A: By blocking the absorption of essential iron supplements
options.B: By triggering inflammation that weakens fetal membranes
options.C: By directly invading the amniotic fluid to cause fetal distress
options.D: By causing a sudden drop in maternal blood pressure

explanation: The body's inflammatory response can release signals that lead to early contractions and cause the bag of waters to break early. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of trichomoniasis during pregnancy?

options.A: Preterm delivery
options.B: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: Premature rupture of membranes
options.D: Low birth weight

explanation: While trichomoniasis is linked to labor complications and early membrane rupture, it does not cause metabolic conditions like gestational diabetes. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h6)

question: What important lifestyle advice must a midwife give a patient prescribed oral metronidazole for trichomoniasis?

options.A: Avoid consuming alcoholic beverages during treatment
options.B: Avoid exposure to direct sunlight while outdoors
options.C: Increase daily fluid intake to four liters
options.D: Stop taking all dairy products for two weeks

explanation: Mixing metronidazole with alcohol causes severe nausea, vomiting, and flushing, so patients must avoid alcohol while taking the medication. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h7)

question: A patient feels worried and ashamed about her diagnosis during an antenatal visit. What is the best initial action for the midwife?

options.A: Insist that she report her sexual partners to local authorities immediately
options.B: Provide a non-judgmental environment and offer supportive counseling
options.C: Refuse to discuss the diagnosis until her partner arrives at the clinic
options.D: Scold her for engaging in risky behaviors before pregnancy

explanation: Creating a safe and supportive space helps reduce stigma, builds trust, and encourages the patient to follow through with her treatment. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T6#BMP116_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is the typical body shape of nematode worms?

options.A: Cylindrical and unsegmented
options.B: Flat and leaf-like
options.C: Segmented and ribbon-like
options.D: Spherical and microscopic

explanation: Nematodes are commonly called roundworms because their bodies are round, cylindrical, and do not have the segments seen in tapeworms. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why are pregnant women in tropical regions often more vulnerable to worm infections?

options.A: Growing fetuses actively attract and feed roundworms
options.B: Prenatal vitamins contain ingredients that nourish intestinal worms
options.C: Normal immune changes during pregnancy lower the body's defense against parasites
options.D: Hormonal surges permanently paralyze the digestive tract

explanation: Pregnancy causes mild changes in the immune system that can make it easier for women to pick up or carry heavier parasite loads. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which worm is most responsible for causing severe iron-deficiency anaemia through blood loss?

options.A: Hookworm
options.B: Whipworm
options.C: Pinworm
options.D: Ascaris

explanation: Hookworms attach to the wall of the gut and feed on the host's blood, making them a major cause of anaemia in pregnancy in endemic areas. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h2)

question: A pregnant woman who walks barefoot on damp soil in a farming community presents with severe anaemia. Which parasite is the likely cause?

options.A: Necator americanus
options.B: Trichuris trichiura
options.C: Ascaris lumbricoides
options.D: Enterobius vermicularis

explanation: Necator americanus is a type of hookworm. Its larvae live in warm, damp soil and infect humans by burrowing through the skin when walking barefoot. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h2)

question: How do people usually catch a hookworm infection from the soil?

options.A: Ingestion of unwashed vegetables
options.B: Active skin penetration by larvae
options.C: Inhalation of airborne eggs
options.D: Vector transmission via mosquito bites

explanation: Unlike roundworms spread by eating contaminated food, hookworm larvae wait in the dirt and crawl directly through human skin, usually through the feet. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h3)

question: Which local practice during pregnancy greatly increases the chance of getting Ascaris or whipworm infections?

options.A: Eating thoroughly cooked bush meat
options.B: Geophagia (eating clay or soil)
options.C: Sleeping without a mosquito net
options.D: Drinking boiled well water

explanation: Eating soil directly introduces infectious worm eggs hiding in the dirt into the pregnant woman's digestive system. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the most common serious complication of a heavy hookworm infection during pregnancy?

options.A: Complete placental abruption
options.B: Severe iron-deficiency anaemia
options.C: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Pregnancy-induced hypertension

explanation: Constant blood loss in the gut to hookworms depletes the mother's iron stores, leading to significant anaemia. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h4)

question: How can a mother's long-term worm infection indirectly affect her newborn baby?

options.A: By triggering immediate congenital limb deformities
options.B: By causing permanent infant blindness at delivery
options.C: By passing active adult worms across the placenta
options.D: By causing fetal growth restriction and low birth weight

explanation: When a mother suffers from ongoing poor nutrition and anaemia due to worms, the baby receives fewer nutrients, which can lead to poor growth. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h4)

question: What is the standard lab test used to confirm an intestinal worm infection?

options.A: Microscopic stool examination for ova
options.B: Fast blood glucose concentration test
options.C: Complete blood count with differential
options.D: Urinalysis for parasite protein markers

explanation: Looking at a stool sample under a microscope allows lab staff to identify the unique eggs laid by adult worms living in the gut. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h5)

question: If a clinic does not have a working microscope for stool tests, what standard public health action is used for pregnant women?

options.A: Presumptive deworming after the first trimester
options.B: Withholding all treatment until after childbirth
options.C: Administering intravenous iron infusions only
options.D: Immediate hospital referral for exploratory surgery

explanation: When testing is not available, health guidelines recommend routine presumptive deworming as part of antenatal care after the first trimester. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h5)

question: During which time in pregnancy is it generally safe to give routine deworming medicine like Albendazole?

options.A: After the first trimester
options.B: Only during the first trimester
options.C: At any point without restriction
options.D: During the first four weeks

explanation: To protect the baby while organs are forming in early pregnancy, routine deworming is delayed until the second trimester and beyond. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why are drugs like Mebendazole considered relatively safe during the second and third trimesters?

options.A: They have low systemic absorption from the gut
options.B: They actively cross the placenta to treat the fetus
options.C: They bind exclusively to maternal fat tissues
options.D: They are completely broken down by stomach acid

explanation: Because very little of the medication enters the mother's bloodstream, the developing baby is barely exposed to the drug. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h6)

question: Which public health step best prevents hookworms from entering through the skin?

options.A: Boiling all drinking water vigorously
options.B: Wearing protective footwear outdoors
options.C: Sleeping under insecticide-treated nets
options.D: Washing hands with soap and water

explanation: Shoes act as a physical barrier, stopping hookworm larvae in the damp soil from burrowing into the skin of the feet. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h7)

question: Why must deworming programs always be paired with teaching about environmental sanitation?

options.A: To prevent rapid reinfection from the contaminated environment
options.B: To eliminate the need for iron and folic acid supplements
options.C: To enhance the chemical potency of deworming tablets
options.D: To stop adult worms from migrating to the lungs

explanation: Without clean water and proper sanitation, treated individuals will quickly pick up new parasites from their surroundings. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T7#BMP116_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary way helminths survive inside a human host?

options.A: Feeding directly on solid bone tissues
options.B: Invading human red blood cells to reproduce
options.C: Absorbing nutrients directly from the host
options.D: Releasing toxic gases into the digestive tract

explanation: Helminths are parasitic worms that live inside the host and take nutrients away from the human body. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why are pregnant women more vulnerable to parasitic worm infections?

options.A: The growing uterus completely blocks worm elimination
options.B: Increased stomach acid provides a breeding ground for larvae
options.C: Normal immune system changes during pregnancy lower resistance
options.D: Hormonal surges permanently destroy intestinal protective linings

explanation: Pregnancy naturally alters immune responses to protect the baby, which makes it easier for parasites to establish themselves. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h1)

question: What is the name of the tapeworm's head used for attaching to the human intestine?

options.A: Proglottid
options.B: Strobila
options.C: Scolex
options.D: Cercaria

explanation: The scolex is the specialized head structure featuring hooks and suckers that anchor the parasite to the gut wall. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h2)

question: How do adult tapeworms obtain their nourishment from the human host?

options.A: Swallowing red blood cells through a central mouth
options.B: Producing their own food via internal chemical organs
options.C: Chewing solid food particles using sharp mouthparts
options.D: Absorbing digested food straight through their skin

explanation: Tapeworms lack a digestive tract entirely, so they absorb nutrients directly across their outer body surface. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h2)

question: Which animal serves as the intermediate host for *Taenia saginata*?

options.A: Snails
options.B: Cattle
options.C: Fish
options.D: Pigs

explanation: Taenia saginata is the beef tapeworm, meaning cattle act as the intermediate host where larval cysts develop in muscle. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h3)

question: What happens when a person accidentally swallows Taenia solium eggs instead of undercooked meat cysts?

options.A: The infection is instantly cleared by normal stomach acid
options.B: Larvae migrate into body tissues to cause cysticercosis
options.C: An adult worm immediately attaches without growing larger
options.D: The person develops lifelong immunity to all other helminths

explanation: Ingesting eggs rather than muscle cysts causes the larvae to hatch, cross the intestinal wall, and form cysts throughout body tissues. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h3)

question: An antenatal patient has chronic fatigue and severe anaemia that does not improve with iron supplements. What underlying parasitic issue should be considered?

options.A: Gestational diabetes blocking proper mineral absorption
options.B: Intestinal tapeworm infection draining vital nutrients
options.C: Acute viral hepatitis affecting liver iron storage
options.D: Normal physiological expansion of maternal blood volume

explanation: Intestinal parasites compete for dietary nutrients and can cause stubborn anaemia that fails to resolve with routine supplementation alone. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h4)

question: Which of the following is a common clinical feature of an intestinal tapeworm?

options.A: Yellow discoloration of the whites of the eyes
options.B: High spiking fevers with severe skin rashes
options.C: Vague abdominal discomfort and weight loss
options.D: Sudden paralysis of the lower extremities

explanation: Tapeworms often cause mild gastrointestinal complaints like abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss despite a normal appetite. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary laboratory method used to confirm an intestinal tapeworm infection?

options.A: Urinalysis using chemical reagent strips
options.B: Measuring fasting blood glucose levels
options.C: Chest X-ray imaging of the lung fields
options.D: Stool microscopy for eggs or proglottids

explanation: Stool microscopy allows laboratory technicians to spot characteristic tapeworm eggs or passed segments. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why might a doctor order repeated stool examinations if the first test result is negative?

options.A: Worms hide inside the stomach lining during the day
options.B: Stool samples must be cultured for at least a week
options.C: Tapeworms shed their diagnostic segments irregularly
options.D: Laboratory reagents expire quickly in warm climates

explanation: Because proglottids and eggs are passed intermittently, a single stool sample might miss the parasite entirely. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is drug treatment for intestinal parasites often delayed until after the first trimester of pregnancy?

options.A: Because parasites naturally die off on their own by week twelve
options.B: Because the maternal stomach cannot absorb drugs early on
options.C: To protect the developing fetus during major organ formation
options.D: To allow the placenta time to filter out chemical toxins

explanation: The first trimester is the critical window of organ development, making it vital to avoid medications that could harm the embryo. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is an important nursing responsibility when managing a pregnant patient diagnosed with a tapeworm infection?

options.A: Stopping all routine antenatal vitamin supplements immediately
options.B: Encouraging complete fasting until all worms are expelled
options.C: Consulting the medical officer to ensure safe timing of drug therapy
options.D: Prescribing high-dose herbal purges without professional review

explanation: Midwives work alongside medical officers to verify that any prescribed treatment is safe for the specific gestational age. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is the most effective household method to kill tapeworm larvae present in raw meat?

options.A: Rinsing the meat surface with cold running water
options.B: Freezing the meat for just one hour before cooking
options.C: Cooking the meat thoroughly until no pink remains
options.D: Soaking the raw meat in vinegar for ten minutes

explanation: Heat destroys the larval cysts embedded in muscle tissue, preventing infection when the meat is consumed. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h7)

question: How does proper community sanitation help break the transmission cycle of tapeworms?

options.A: It eliminates flies that carry tapeworm eggs onto drinking water
options.B: It stops livestock from ingesting human faeces containing eggs
options.C: It prevents adult worms from leaving the human host's body
options.D: It neutralizes chemical pollutants in the local soil and crops

explanation: Sanitary latrines keep human waste away from animals like pigs and cattle, breaking the cycle where animals ingest parasite eggs. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T8#BMP116_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is the common name given to trematodes?

options.A: Flukes
options.B: Pinworms
options.C: Roundworms
options.D: Tapeworms

explanation: Trematodes are parasitic flatworms commonly referred to as flukes that affect various organs in the human body. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why must Nigerian midwives understand parasitic worm infections during antenatal care?

options.A: Helminths are the primary cause of all pregnancy complications
options.B: Midwives are solely responsible for vector control in rivers
options.C: Routine delivery suites require parasite disinfection
options.D: Infections can severely affect the health of both mother and fetus

explanation: Parasitic infections during pregnancy can lead to severe anemia and adverse birth outcomes, making maternal awareness vital. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which physical feature is characteristic of trematode anatomy?

options.A: Cylindrical tapered round bodies
options.B: Long segmented ribbon-like bodies
options.C: Hard chitinous exoskeleton
options.D: Leaf-shaped flat body with suckers

explanation: Trematodes are known for their flattened, leaf-like appearance and muscular suckers used for tissue attachment. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h2)

question: Which trematode group is unique for having separate male and female sexes?

options.A: Liver flukes
options.B: Schistosomes
options.C: Intestinal flukes
options.D: Lung flukes

explanation: Unlike most other trematodes which are hermaphrodites, blood flukes or schistosomes exist as distinct male and female worms. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h2)

question: What animal serves as the mandatory intermediate host for human-infecting trematodes?

options.A: Freshwater snail
options.B: Domestic cattle
options.C: Freshwater fish
options.D: Female Anopheles mosquito

explanation: Freshwater snails are required intermediate hosts where trematodes undergo essential stages of development and multiplication. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h3)

question: How do humans typically contract schistosomiasis during daily activities?

options.A: Eating raw or undercooked freshwater vegetation
options.B: Inhaling dust particles near dried riverbeds
options.C: Swimming or wading in water containing infective cercariae
options.D: Being bitten by infected blood-sucking flies

explanation: Infective larval forms called cercariae actively penetrate human skin when people come into contact with contaminated natural water bodies. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h3)

question: Where do adult Schistosoma haematobium worms primarily live in the human body?

options.A: Bladder venous plexus
options.B: Bowel mesenteric venules
options.C: Bile ducts of the liver
options.D: Blood vessels of the lungs

explanation: Schistosoma haematobium prefers the veins surrounding the urinary bladder, which leads to urinary symptoms such as blood in the urine. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h4)

question: What is the classic clinical sign of urinary schistosomiasis seen in affected individuals?

options.A: Terminal hematuria
options.B: Jaundice and yellow eyes
options.C: Persistent dry coughing
options.D: Severe watery diarrhea

explanation: The passage of blood at the very end of urination is a hallmark sign of bladder damage caused by Schistosoma haematobium eggs. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why does tissue damage occur primarily in chronic schistosomiasis infections?

options.A: Adult worms release large amounts of toxic digestive enzymes
options.B: Larvae consume red blood cells directly inside major arteries
options.C: The body mounts an immune reaction against trapped parasite eggs
options.D: The intermediate snail host injects poisonous venom into the blood

explanation: Granulomas and scarring form when the host immune system reacts strongly to eggs that fail to exit the body and become trapped in organs. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h5)

question: A pregnant woman in a rural clinic presents with chronic anemia and blood in her urine. Which complication is she most at risk for if left untreated?

options.A: Complete blockage of the upper respiratory tract
options.B: Low birth weight and poor fetal growth
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: Rapid onset gestational diabetes mellitus

explanation: Severe maternal anemia and chronic pelvic pathology from schistosomiasis frequently compromise placental oxygenation and nutrient delivery to the fetus. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the standard laboratory method for diagnosing urinary schistosomiasis?

options.A: Culture of blood samples on nutrient agar plates
options.B: Rapid diagnostic test detecting salivary antigens
options.C: Ultrasound scanning of the maternal abdomen
options.D: Microscopic examination of centrifuged terminal urine

explanation: Spinning a terminal urine sample concentrates the heavy eggs, making them visible under a microscope during examination. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h6)

question: Which stool examination technique is commonly used to quantify Schistosoma mansoni eggs?

options.A: Direct saline wet mount only
options.B: Gram stain and culture
options.C: Kato-Katz thick smear
options.D: Acid-fast staining method

explanation: The Kato-Katz technique provides a standardized way to process stool samples and count helminth eggs for diagnosis. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary medication recommended for treating schistosomiasis?

options.A: Chloroquine
options.B: Metronidazole
options.C: Praziquantel
options.D: Benzylpenicillin

explanation: Praziquantel is the safe and highly effective broad-spectrum antihelminthic used globally to treat all species of schistosomes. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h7)

question: How has modern clinical guidance evolved regarding the use of Praziquantel during pregnancy?

options.A: It is considered safe to use during all trimesters when indicated
options.B: It must be completely avoided until breastfeeding has finished
options.C: It is only permitted during the first four weeks of gestation
options.D: It requires surgical removal of worms alongside drug therapy

explanation: Updated evidence shows that treating pregnant women with Praziquantel prevents severe maternal complications without harming the fetus. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h7)

question: Why is health education about water contact essential for controlling schistosomiasis in rural communities?

options.A: It teaches mothers how to purify water using expensive laboratory filters
options.B: It completely replaces the need for medical deworming tablets
options.C: It helps villagers break the transmission cycle by avoiding infested water
options.D: It cures chronic liver scarring caused by long-term infections

explanation: Educating communities on safe water habits stops parasites from entering water sources and infecting new hosts. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h8)

question: A midwife is planning outreach activities in a riverine community with high schistosomiasis rates. Which strategy should be included to ensure sustainable control?

options.A: Spraying dangerous chemical pesticides inside local residential homes
options.B: Participating in community mass drug administration and sanitation awareness
options.C: Advising pregnant women to stop drinking all forms of liquid entirely
options.D: Treating only male adults since they work more often in rivers

explanation: Combining mass drug treatment with community-wide health education on hygiene creates a sustainable defense against reinfection. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T9#BMP116_U3_T9_h8)

question: Why do viruses rely completely on host cells to survive?

options.A: They are too large to survive outside of human blood vessels
options.B: They can only reproduce when exposed to direct sunlight
options.C: They possess thick cell walls made of peptidoglycan
options.D: They completely lack their own metabolic machinery and energy production

explanation: Viruses do not have the cellular structures needed to make energy or proteins independently, forcing them to invade living cells. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why do standard antibiotics fail to treat viral infections?

options.A: Antibiotics target bacterial structures like cell walls that viruses do not possess
options.B: Antibiotics are quickly destroyed by the immune system of pregnant women
options.C: Bacterial cells are much smaller than any known viral particle
options.D: Viruses hide inside red blood cells where drugs cannot reach them

explanation: Antibiotics disrupt bacterial processes, but viruses use completely different structures and host machinery, making antibacterial drugs ineffective. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is the protective protein coat that surrounds the genetic material of a virus called?

options.A: Peptidoglycan
options.B: Capsid
options.C: Ribosome
options.D: Cellulose

explanation: The capsid is the protein shell that protects the viral nucleic acid core from damage. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which type of virus is usually easier to destroy by simple handwashing with soap or alcohol?

options.A: Bacterial spores
options.B: Fungal yeasts
options.C: Enveloped viruses
options.D: Naked viruses

explanation: Enveloped viruses rely on a fragile lipid membrane that is easily dissolved by soap and alcohol, rendering the virus inactive. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h2)

question: What unique enzyme do retroviruses like HIV use to convert their genetic material inside a host cell?

options.A: DNA polymerase
options.B: Amylase
options.C: Reverse transcriptase
options.D: Peptidase

explanation: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase to transcribe their single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA inside the host cell. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is the main basis of the Baltimore classification system for viruses?

options.A: The specific organ in the human body that the virus infects
options.B: The physical size of the viral capsid and tail fibers
options.C: The type of nucleic acid and how it makes messenger RNA
options.D: Whether the virus causes acute or chronic clinical illness

explanation: The Baltimore system organizes viruses primarily by their genome structure and replication strategy, specifically focusing on mRNA production. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h3)

question: During which stage of viral replication is the protein coat stripped away to expose the genetic material?

options.A: Budding
options.B: Attachment
options.C: Uncoating
options.D: Assembly

explanation: Uncoating is the specific step where the capsid breaks down or opens up inside the cell to release the viral genome. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h4)

question: An antiviral drug stops a virus from binding to surface receptors on a human cell. Which replication stage is this drug targeting?

options.A: Attachment
options.B: Uncoating
options.C: Biosynthesis
options.D: Release

explanation: Drugs that block surface binding prevent the very first step of viral entry, known as attachment or adsorption. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h4)

question: What term describes the visible structural changes or damage in host cells infected by a virus?

options.A: Phagocytic lysis
options.B: Cytopathic effect
options.C: Osmotic pressure
options.D: Bacterial conjugation

explanation: Cytopathic effect refers to the recognizable damage or abnormalities produced in host cells due to viral invasion and replication. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h5)

question: How do latent viral infections differ from acute viral infections in the body?

options.A: Latent viruses never trigger any immune response from the pregnant mother
options.B: Latent viruses can remain inside host cells quietly for a long time without causing immediate cell destruction
options.C: Latent viruses are easily cured by standard doses of common antibiotics
options.D: Latent viruses only attack red blood cells while acute viruses attack white blood cells

explanation: Latent infections hide silently within tissues and can reactivate later, whereas acute infections usually produce rapid multiplication and symptoms. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T1#BMP116_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why do viruses need to invade a living host cell?

options.A: They feed directly on red blood cells for energy
options.B: They cannot survive outside of oxygen-rich environments
options.C: They lack the cellular machinery for independent survival
options.D: They need high temperatures found inside blood vessels

explanation: Viruses cannot multiply on their own because they lack the internal machinery needed to make copies of themselves. They must hijack a host cell to replicate. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is it important for midwives to understand viral infections?

options.A: Many viral infections can cross the placenta and harm the fetus
options.B: Viral illnesses only affect pregnant women in tropical climates
options.C: Midwives are solely responsible for manufacturing viral vaccines
options.D: Viruses can be easily cured using standard broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Certain viruses can pass from the mother to the baby during pregnancy or birth, making it important for midwives to recognize and prevent these risks. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is a main feature of DNA viruses compared to RNA viruses?

options.A: They require bacterial cells to complete their life cycle
options.B: They generally have lower mutation rates than RNA viruses
options.C: They are completely unresponsive to human immune responses
options.D: They replicate exclusively in the cytoplasm of host cells

explanation: DNA viruses tend to mutate more slowly because their copying enzymes have built-in proofreading features that catch and fix errors. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h2)

question: A pregnant woman has active genital herpes near her delivery date. What is the main concern for the baby?

options.A: Immediate need to administer high doses of routine bacterial antibiotics
options.B: Permanent immunity for the infant against all viral respiratory infections
options.C: Certain development of congenital hearing loss in the unborn baby
options.D: Risk of transmitting the virus to the newborn during a vaginal birth

explanation: Active herpes lesions during labor pose a risk of passing the virus to the baby, which is why precautions like a cesarean section are often considered. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h2)

question: Why do RNA viruses mutate much faster than DNA viruses?

options.A: They live outside human host cells for extended periods
options.B: Their replication enzymes usually lack proofreading mechanisms
options.C: They reproduce much slower, giving more time for errors
options.D: They combine their genetic material directly with bacteria

explanation: RNA virus copying enzymes make mistakes without checking them. These copying errors add up quickly, causing the virus to mutate often. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which RNA virus can cause severe liver failure, especially in pregnant women?

options.A: Hepatitis E Virus
options.B: Herpes Simplex Virus
options.C: Cytomegalovirus
options.D: Influenza Virus

explanation: Hepatitis E is known to carry a high risk of severe liver complications, particularly during the third trimester of pregnancy. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why are pregnant women more vulnerable to certain viral infections?

options.A: An excessive overproduction of white blood cells
options.B: Partial maternal immune tolerance to protect the fetus
options.C: The permanent loss of mucosal membrane barriers
options.D: A complete shutdown of the lymphatic system

explanation: The immune system naturally adjusts during pregnancy so it does not reject the baby, which can slightly lower defense against some viruses. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why should pregnant women avoid contact with people who have active viral rashes?

options.A: Rashes always indicate a severe bacterial infection requiring strong antibiotics
options.B: Viral pathogens can spread easily and potentially harm the developing fetus
options.C: Skin rashes interfere directly with normal maternal blood pressure control
options.D: Pregnant women are immune to all forms of skin-related infections

explanation: Many rash-causing viruses spread easily through close contact and can cross the placenta, leading to potential complications for the baby. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which type of vaccine is avoided during pregnancy due to the risk of fetal infection?

options.A: Toxoid bacterial vaccines
options.B: Live attenuated vaccines
options.C: Recombinant subunit vaccines
options.D: Inactivated viral vaccines

explanation: Live vaccines use a weakened form of the live virus. While safe for most people, they are avoided in pregnancy because they could potentially cross the placenta. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is supportive care the main treatment approach for most viral infections?

options.A: Specific antiviral medications are limited and antibiotics do not kill viruses
options.B: Supportive care permanently alters human DNA to resist future infections
options.C: Viruses always disappear completely within twenty-four hours without care
options.D: Hospitals lack the equipment required to test for viral pathogens

explanation: Antibiotics only fight bacteria and specific antiviral drugs are scarce, so treatment focuses on relieving symptoms while the body heals itself. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T2#BMP116_U4_T2_h5)

question: What does the term hepatitis mean?

options.A: Failure of the gallbladder
options.B: Inflammation of the liver
options.C: Swelling of the kidneys
options.D: Infection of the placenta

explanation: Hepatitis simply means inflammation of the liver tissue, which can be caused by viruses or other factors. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why are pregnant women extra vulnerable to certain strains of hepatitis?

options.A: Pregnancy permanently stops viral replication in the bloodstream
options.B: Normal pregnancy hormones completely neutralize liver enzymes
options.C: Pregnancy makes the liver more prone to severe disease
options.D: The fetus protects the maternal liver from any lasting damage

explanation: Certain viruses like Hepatitis E can cause very severe liver issues because of the unique physical stress of pregnancy. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h1)

question: How does the Hepatitis A virus usually spread?

options.A: Via unprotected sexual intercourse
options.B: Through the fecal-oral route
options.C: Through infected blood transfusions
options.D: By direct mosquito bites

explanation: Hepatitis A spreads when a person eats or drinks something contaminated with tiny amounts of infected stool. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h2)

question: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks gets Hepatitis A. What is the usual outcome for her liver after recovery?

options.A: Delayed progression to primary liver cancer
options.B: Complete recovery without chronic carrier state
options.C: Lifelong shedding of the virus in her stool
options.D: Development of permanent liver cirrhosis

explanation: Hepatitis A is an acute infection that usually heals completely on its own, leaving the patient with lifelong immunity and no long-term liver trouble. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the main way Hepatitis B passes from mother to baby during childbirth?

options.A: Transmission through casual touch in the clinic
options.B: Inhalation of respiratory droplets in the ward
options.C: Consuming poorly cooked meat during labor
options.D: Perinatal transmission from mother to baby

explanation: Babies can pick up the virus when they come into contact with maternal blood and body fluids while passing through the birth canal. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is it urgent to treat a newborn quickly if born to an HBsAg-positive mother?

options.A: Babies infected at birth have a very high risk of chronic disease
options.B: Maternal antibodies block all future routine vaccinations
options.C: Innate immunity in infants is too weak to clear the virus
options.D: The newborn liver grows rapidly and needs immediate protection

explanation: Giving quick treatment helps stop the virus from turning into a permanent, lifelong infection in the baby. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which test confirms an active Hepatitis C infection after a positive screening?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Liver biopsy procedure
options.C: HCV RNA PCR test
options.D: Urinalysis strip test

explanation: This molecular test checks for the virus's genetic material in the blood to confirm an active infection. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why is testing a newborn for Hepatitis C antibodies right after birth unreliable?

options.A: Viral particles destroy all blood cells before they can be counted
options.B: Colostrum contains substances that neutralize testing reagents
options.C: The newborn liver does not produce antibodies until school age
options.D: Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and persist in the infant

explanation: Antibodies from an infected mother stay in the baby's blood for months, which can make it look like the baby is infected when they are not. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h4)

question: What must be given to a newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother within 24 hours of birth?

options.A: Broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
options.B: Vitamin K injection only
options.C: Antiviral syrup for ten days
options.D: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG

explanation: Giving both the vaccine and the immune globulin right away gives the baby immediate and long-term defense against the virus. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h5)

question: A pregnant woman tests negative for Hepatitis B surface antigen at her booking visit. What is the best midwifery action?

options.A: Offer the Hepatitis B vaccine series if she is not yet immunized
options.B: Prescribe therapeutic antiviral drugs for daily pregnancy use
options.C: Isolate her from other pregnant women in the antenatal ward
options.D: Repeat the antibody screening test every single week

explanation: If she does not have the virus and is not yet vaccinated, offering the vaccine during pregnancy helps keep her safe. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T3#BMP116_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which immune cells are the main target of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)?

options.A: Platelets
options.B: CD4+ T-lymphocytes
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: Neutrophils

explanation: HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which progressively weakens the body's immune defenses. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h1)

question: How does the loss of coordinator immune cells affect an infected person?

options.A: It permanently prevents bacterial growth
options.B: It causes rapid red blood cell production
options.C: It immediately causes total paralysis
options.D: It leaves the body open to opportunistic infections

explanation: Without coordinator cells to direct the immune response, the body cannot defend itself against common germs, leading to opportunistic infections. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h1)

question: What enzyme does HIV use to convert its RNA into DNA inside a host cell?

options.A: Reverse transcriptase
options.B: Lipase
options.C: Amylase
options.D: Pepsin

explanation: Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme retroviruses use to transcribe their single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h2)

question: At what point is an HIV-positive individual formally diagnosed with AIDS?

options.A: When the CD4 count drops severely or AIDS-defining illnesses appear
options.B: When the virus completely disappears from blood
options.C: As soon as antibodies are found on a screening test
options.D: During the first week after initial exposure

explanation: AIDS represents the advanced stage of HIV infection characterized by a low CD4 count and specific marker conditions. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h2)

question: What is the main action of oncogenic viruses in the human body?

options.A: They cure existing bacterial infections
options.B: They stop all cellular replication
options.C: They alter host cell DNA to cause uncontrolled cell division
options.D: They rapidly destroy all red blood cells

explanation: Oncogenic viruses modify the genetic material of host cells, bypassing normal growth controls and leading to cancer. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h3)

question: How do Hepatitis B and C lead to liver cancer over time?

options.A: By causing chronic inflammation and continuous tissue regeneration
options.B: By freezing all metabolic processes in liver cells
options.C: By stopping the production of bile
options.D: By replacing liver tissue with bone marrow

explanation: Long-term liver inflammation forces constant cell repair and division, increasing the chance of permanent genetic errors and cancer. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why are people living with HIV at a higher risk of developing virus-induced cancers?

options.A: A weakened immune system fails to clear secondary viral infections
options.B: The virus produces toxins that destroy tumor suppressors
options.C: HIV turns every human organ into a tumor
options.D: Antiretroviral drugs cause rapid cell growth

explanation: A depleted immune system cannot control other viruses, allowing cancer-linked strains to multiply and transform host cells. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a virus linked to HIV-associated cancers?

options.A: Human Papillomavirus
options.B: Hepatitis B virus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Influenza virus

explanation: Influenza causes acute respiratory illness and is not classified as an oncogenic virus linked to malignancies. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h4)

question: What viral agent causes Kaposi sarcoma in immunocompromised patients?

options.A: Varicella-zoster virus
options.B: Human Herpesvirus 8
options.C: Cytomegalovirus
options.D: Rabies virus

explanation: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) is the specific pathogen required for the development of Kaposi sarcoma lesions. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h5)

question: A patient living with HIV has distinctive purplish skin and oral lesions. What condition is this?

options.A: Kaposi sarcoma
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Pneumococcal pneumonia
options.D: Acute malaria

explanation: Purplish vascular lesions on the skin and mucous membranes are classic clinical signs of Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of giving Antiretroviral Therapy to pregnant women living with HIV?

options.A: To increase red blood cell counts
options.B: To replace routine blood pressure checks
options.C: To achieve viral suppression and prevent mother-to-child transmission
options.D: To cure all bacterial infections

explanation: Lowering the viral load through ART protects the mother's health and reduces the chance of transmitting HIV to the baby. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h6)

question: During antenatal clinic duties, what key preventive service should a midwife promote to protect young girls against cervical cancer?

options.A: Routine chest radiography
options.B: Daily iron and folate supplementation
options.C: Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: Human Papillomavirus vaccination

explanation: Administering the HPV vaccine to young adolescent girls before sexual debut is an effective primary prevention strategy against cervical cancer. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T4#BMP116_U4_T4_h6)

question: What do viruses need to hijack in order to multiply?

options.A: Maternal red blood cells
options.B: Extracellular fluid matrix
options.C: Host cell machinery
options.D: Placental villi tissue

explanation: Viruses cannot make copies of themselves on their own. They rely completely on the inner workings of a host cell to produce more viral particles. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is getting a viral infection in early pregnancy often more dangerous for the baby than later on?

options.A: Maternal antibodies are completely absent early on
options.B: Fetal liver enzymes neutralize viruses poorly at term
options.C: Organogenesis happens during the first trimester
options.D: The placenta is fully permeable only in early pregnancy

explanation: The first trimester is when the baby's vital organs are actively forming. Because cells are dividing rapidly to build these organs, viral disruption during this time causes more severe structural damage. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which test directly looks for the actual genetic material of a virus in a sample?

options.A: Routine full blood count analysis
options.B: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: Immunoglobulin G antibody titers
options.D: Polymerase Chain Reaction testing

explanation: PCR tests zoom in on specific viral RNA or DNA sequences, making it a very sensitive way to catch active infections. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h2)

question: In an antenatal client, what does finding IgM antibodies usually point to?

options.A: Chronic asymptomatic viral colonization
options.B: A recent or acute primary infection
options.C: Total clearance of all viral pathogens
options.D: Long-term immunity from past vaccination

explanation: IgM is the body's first responder antibody. When it shows up in a blood test, it tells us a brand-new infection has recently occurred. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which routine blood test screens pregnant women for chronic Hepatitis B?

options.A: Hepatitis C viral culture
options.B: Hepatitis E core protein
options.C: Hepatitis A total antibodies
options.D: Hepatitis B surface antigen

explanation: Checking for the Hepatitis B surface antigen helps midwives spot mothers who currently carry the virus and might pass it to their baby. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h3)

question: A pregnant woman's screening shows high IgG but no IgM for an infection. What does this mean?

options.A: Her unborn baby is currently infected in utero
options.B: She has past immunity from a previous infection
options.C: The laboratory sample was contaminated in transit
options.D: She has an active acute infection right now

explanation: Finding IgG without IgM means the exposure happened before this pregnancy, leaving her with safe baseline immunity. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h3)

question: How do antiviral medicines called nucleoside analogues stop viruses from spreading?

options.A: By dissolving the outer lipid envelope
options.B: By blocking placental nutrient exchange
options.C: By stimulating maternal white blood cells
options.D: By disrupting viral DNA building blocks

explanation: These medications sneak faulty pieces into the virus's building blocks, stopping the replication cycle in its tracks. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why do healthcare providers use a combination of drugs to treat chronic HIV instead of just one?

options.A: Combination regimens eliminate the need for lab tests
options.B: Single drugs are completely inactive in pregnancy
options.C: Combination therapy prevents rapid viral resistance
options.D: Single medications cause severe maternal kidney failure

explanation: Using multiple drugs at once makes it much harder for the virus to mutate and figure out a way around the treatment. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h4)

question: Without medical intervention, when is an HIV-positive mother most likely to pass the virus to her baby?

options.A: During third trimester sleep
options.B: During labor and delivery
options.C: During the first trimester
options.D: During pre-conception weeks

explanation: The process of birth involves direct contact with maternal blood and genital secretions, carrying the highest risk for passing the virus along. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h5)

question: An HIV-positive mother with a low viral load just delivered a healthy baby. What is the priority action for the midwifery team?

options.A: Withholding all early feeding for forty-eight hours
options.B: Isolating the infant in a specialized nursery
options.C: Bathing the newborn in antiseptic solutions
options.D: Administering infant antiretroviral prophylaxis

explanation: Giving the baby early antiretroviral medicine helps clear out any virus they might have been exposed to during birth. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of pre-test counseling before a pregnant woman takes a viral screening test?

options.A: To enforce mandatory isolation of infected persons
options.B: To prepare the client and obtain informed consent
options.C: To calculate the exact date of fetal conception
options.D: To diagnose the infection before blood is drawn

explanation: Pre-test counseling ensures the mother understands why the test is happening and agrees to take it of her own free will. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the best way to share complex test results with a pregnant client?

options.A: Handing over a medical textbook chapter to read
options.B: Directing all questions exclusively to her partner
options.C: Relying entirely on written pamphlets without talking
options.D: Using simple language and checking for understanding

explanation: Talking openly in plain language helps lower anxiety and makes sure the mother truly understands her health and care plan. [learn more](BMP116_U4_T5#BMP116_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why do midwives use standard precautions for every single patient in the labour ward?

options.A: Hospital regulations require paperwork for every single birth.
options.B: It is impossible to wash hands without following standard rules.
options.C: Midwives only need protection when treating high-risk mothers.
options.D: Any patient can potentially carry and transmit infectious pathogens.

explanation: Standard precautions assume that body fluids from any person may contain infectious agents, so safety measures apply universally to protect both patients and healthcare workers. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T1#BMP116_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which procedure breaks the body's natural barrier against microorganisms?

options.A: Checking the mother's blood pressure with a cuff
options.B: Performing an episiotomy or repairing a tear
options.C: Handing clean linen to the mother after delivery
options.D: Listening to fetal heart tones using a Doppler device

explanation: Procedures that cut or pierce the skin and mucous membranes break the natural defense barrier, creating a direct entry route for bacteria. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T1#BMP116_U5_T1_h1)

question: What must be completely destroyed during a valid sterilization process?

options.A: Visible dirt and dried blood stains on metal surfaces
options.B: All microorganisms including bacterial endospores
options.C: Fungi and viruses while ignoring bacterial spores
options.D: Only active bacteria floating on the instrument surface

explanation: Sterilization is an absolute state meaning zero living organisms or spores remain on the processed item. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T1#BMP116_U5_T1_h2)

question: Why must instruments used for a caesarean section be sterilized instead of simply disinfected?

options.A: Boiling water damages the sharp cutting edges of surgical scissors.
options.B: They enter deep, sterile tissues where any surviving microbe can cause severe infection.
options.C: Surgeons prefer shiny metal tools that have been baked in dry heat ovens.
options.D: Disinfection takes too much time during a busy theatre operating schedule.

explanation: Items touching sterile internal body cavities require complete elimination of all microbial life to prevent deep-seated wound sepsis. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T1#BMP116_U5_T1_h2)
